sections.title: Compare two routes of coordination
paragraphs: Nervous communication uses electrical impulses along neurones and, at the chemical synapses studied here, neurotransmitters between cells. Hormonal communication uses chemical messengers released by endocrine glands into the blood, which carries them to target cells.

Nervous pathways can give a rapid, directed response in a particular connected effector. Endocrine hormones circulate more widely, but only cells with suitable receptors respond; being carried past a cell does not make that cell a target.

The usual school comparison describes nervous effects as faster and shorter lasting, and hormonal effects as slower and longer lasting. These are general patterns rather than absolute rules: adrenaline can rapidly affect several organs, and nervous activity can have prolonged consequences.

The systems can work together. Nervous input can stimulate adrenal hormone release, while hormonal feedback can influence coordinating centres. Do not describe hormones as electrical impulses travelling in blood.

example.question: Why can a hormone circulate widely without changing every cell?
steps: Blood distributes the chemical messenger.
Only target cells with suitable receptors respond to that messenger.
Distribution and response specificity are different parts of the explanation.
example.explanation: Compare messenger, transport route and target before describing typical speed and duration.

practice.question: Does rapid adrenaline action prove it is a nerve impulse?
practice.answer: No. Adrenaline is a hormone carried in blood; speed alone does not identify the communication route.
practice.explanation: Compare messenger, transport route and target before describing typical speed and duration.

commonMistakes: Do not say all hormones act slowly or every cell responds to each circulating hormone.

sections.title: Identify the central nervous system
paragraphs: The central nervous system, or CNS, consists of the brain and spinal cord. Nerves link it to sense organs and effectors in the rest of the body.

A neurone is a nerve cell. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres, mainly axons, outside the CNS; the words do not refer to the same level of organisation. A nerve can contain fibres carrying sensory information towards the CNS and motor information away from it.

The spinal cord is nervous tissue inside the vertebral column. It is not the bony backbone itself. The brain and cord receive, integrate and relay information; some simple responses can be coordinated in the spinal cord.

example.question: A diagram labels the brain, spinal cord and a nerve to a hand. Which labels are the CNS?
steps: Brain and spinal cord are the CNS.
The hand nerve links the CNS with the body.
The vertebral bones protect the cord but are not nervous tissue.
example.explanation: Use the CNS boundary and distinguish cell, fibre bundle and protective bone.

practice.question: Is a whole nerve a single neurone?
practice.answer: No. A nerve contains many nerve fibres; a neurone is one cell.
practice.explanation: Use the CNS boundary and distinguish cell, fibre bundle and protective bone.

commonMistakes: Do not replace spinal cord with vertebral column or classify every nerve as part of the CNS.

sections.title: Follow incoming and outgoing impulses
paragraphs: Stimulation of a receptor in a sense organ leads to electrical signals in a sensory pathway. Sensory neurones carry impulses towards the CNS. Processing within the CNS can lead to impulses in motor neurones travelling towards an effector.

For a muscular response, the effector contracts and produces movement. Some responses involve glands changing secretion. The receptor detects the stimulus; it does not itself perform the muscular response.

The speed of impulse transmission helps give rapid responses. An impulse is a change travelling along a neurone membrane, not a small piece of blood carrying electricity and not a hormone flowing through the neurone.

Use the direction relative to the CNS, rather than the left/right direction on a drawing, to distinguish sensory from motor. A nerve drawn pointing upwards can contain fibres with different functional directions.

example.question: A signal travels from a skin receptor towards the spinal cord. Which type of neurone carries this part?
steps: This is a sensory neurone because the direction is towards the CNS.
The outgoing route to a muscle uses a motor neurone.
The muscle, not either nerve cell, is the contracting effector.
example.explanation: Name each pathway by its direction relative to the CNS.

practice.question: A motor fibre is drawn on the left of a diagram. Does left mean sensory?
practice.answer: No. Motor describes impulses travelling away from the CNS to an effector, regardless of page position.
practice.explanation: Name each pathway by its direction relative to the CNS.

commonMistakes: Do not swap sensory and motor or transport nerve impulses in blood.

sections.title: Explain transmission across a synapse
paragraphs: A synapse is a junction between a neurone and another cell. At a chemical synapse, a narrow synaptic cleft separates the sending nerve ending from the receiving membrane.

An arriving electrical impulse triggers release of neurotransmitter from vesicles in the sending ending. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to suitable receptor proteins on the receiving cell.

At an excitatory synapse, this changes the receiving membrane and can initiate a new electrical impulse if sufficient stimulation is reached. Some neurotransmitter effects are inhibitory; it is not correct to say every released molecule always starts an impulse.

The chemical signal is then removed, for example by breakdown or reuptake, so its effect does not continue indefinitely. The electrical impulse does not jump unchanged across the gap, and diffusion of neurotransmitter is not diffusion of an electrical impulse.

example.question: Put the main chemical-synapse events in order.
steps: Electrical impulse reaches the sending ending.
Neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across the cleft.
It binds to receptor proteins on the receiving membrane.
An excitatory effect can lead to a new impulse; the neurotransmitter is later cleared.
example.explanation: Separate electrical signalling along cells from chemical transmission between them.

practice.question: What physically crosses the cleft in this model?
practice.answer: Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across it. The electrical signal is regenerated in the next neurone when sufficiently stimulated.
practice.explanation: Separate electrical signalling along cells from chemical transmission between them.

commonMistakes: Do not say the two neurones touch across the cleft or electricity diffuses like a molecule.

sections.title: Explain direction at a chemical junction
paragraphs: In the usual chemical-synapse model, the sending ending contains release vesicles and the receiving membrane has the relevant receptors. This arrangement helps transmission proceed from the sending side to the receiving side.

Releasing, diffusing and binding the chemical messenger adds a delay compared with transmission along a continuous fibre. Rapid responses are still possible; a delay does not mean the whole response is slow.

A chemical-synapse receptor is a molecule on a membrane. A sensory receptor is a cell or ending that detects a stimulus. They share the idea of detection but are not interchangeable labels in a reflex diagram.
This explanation is specifically for the chemical synapses required here. It does not assert that every junction in every nervous system uses the same mechanism.

example.question: Why does reversing an arrow not reverse a chemical synapse’s function?
steps: An arrow is only a representation.
The release machinery and receiving receptors determine the functional direction.
Changing the drawing does not swap those structures.
example.explanation: Relate direction and timing to the structures at the junction.

practice.question: Does neurotransmitter removal mean it travels along the motor axon to the muscle?
practice.answer: No. Clearance acts at the synapse; an electrical impulse travels along the next neurone.
practice.explanation: Relate direction and timing to the structures at the junction.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse a membrane binding site with the whole skin receptor in the stimulus pathway.

sections.title: Trace a finger-withdrawal reflex
paragraphs: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. In the simple withdrawal model, receptors in the skin detect a harmful hot stimulus and impulses travel along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord.

Within the spinal cord, synapses connect the sensory pathway to a relay neurone and then to a motor neurone. Motor impulses travel to the relevant arm muscles. These muscles contract to withdraw the finger from the hot object.

The pathway is stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the spinal cord → motor neurone → muscle effector → withdrawal. The synapses use neurotransmitters, while the impulses along the neurones are electrical.

The spinal response does not have to wait for a conscious decision by the brain. Information can also travel to the brain, giving awareness of pain; saying that the brain never receives information would be wrong. The model omits the full network and opposing-muscle control.

example.question: Explain how a finger can start withdrawing before a deliberate decision.
steps: Skin receptors detect the harmful stimulus.
Sensory impulses reach a spinal circuit with relay and motor neurones.
Motor impulses cause an arm-muscle effector to contract.
The response does not wait for conscious choice; information can still reach the brain.
example.explanation: Trace the stimulus to the contracting effector and distinguish coordination from conscious choice.

practice.question: Is the effector the spinal cord or the contracting arm muscle?
practice.answer: The muscle is the effector. The spinal cord coordinates the simple pathway.
practice.explanation: Trace the stimulus to the contracting effector and distinguish coordination from conscious choice.

commonMistakes: Do not omit the receptor/effector, reverse the neurones or claim that no CNS is involved.

diagram.alt: Original functional withdrawal pathway: harmful hot stimulus, skin receptor, sensory neurone into a spinal-cord relay circuit, motor neurone to an arm-muscle effector, then finger withdrawal. A separate branch conveys information towards the brain. Synapses within the spinal circuit are chemical.
diagram.caption: Original functional model, not anatomical positions or a measured response-time diagram. Awareness can accompany the spinal response without being a prerequisite for withdrawal.

sections.title: Use function to label an unfamiliar pathway
paragraphs: Label a reflex diagram from the connections and arrow direction. The sensory neurone brings receptor information to the CNS; the relay neurone links within the CNS; the motor neurone carries output to the effector.

Typical sensory-neurone drawings show a cell body off the long conducting route; motor-neurone drawings show a cell body at one end with branching inputs and a long axon towards the muscle. These sketches are models, not a rule that every nerve cell has identical geometry.

A signal interruption before the spinal circuit can prevent that input from reaching it; an interruption on the motor route can prevent that output reaching the muscle even if sensory information reaches the CNS. State the precise segment and observed outcome rather than diagnosing an injury from a simple diagram.
Do not test this response using painful heat. For the hot-object example, use a diagram or described observation; the library has not performed a physical withdrawal experiment.

example.question: A diagram’s receptor-to-CNS arrow is reversed by mistake. How would you repair it?
steps: Sensory impulses should be shown from the receptor towards the CNS.
Motor impulses should be shown from the CNS towards the muscle.
Place the relay within the spinal circuit for this example.
example.explanation: Use topology and functional direction to interpret the diagram safely.

practice.question: Does a nerve pathway that bends down on the page have to be a motor pathway?
practice.answer: No. Use its origin, destination and functional direction, not its drawing angle.
practice.explanation: Use topology and functional direction to interpret the diagram safely.

commonMistakes: Do not infer nerve-cell role from colour or page position alone, or propose a painful heat test.

sections.title: Distinguish a reflex from a deliberate reaction
paragraphs: Withdrawing from a harmful hot surface is the specified automatic reflex example. Seeing a dropped ruler and deliberately closing the fingers is a reaction involving perception and a chosen response; it is not the same simple spinal withdrawal arc.
Both can use nervous pathways, so “nervous” does not mean “reflex”. A reflex is characterised by automatic coordination of its pathway; conscious awareness may still occur during or after it.

A shorter pathway and rapid impulse conduction can support quick protection, but no universal response time follows from the simple model. Actual timings depend on pathway, stimulus and measurement method.
If comparing observations, keep stimulus, response definition and measurement conditions clear. Do not invent trial times or infer hormonal communication just because a measured reaction is slower.

example.question: Is a ruler-catching task a direct measurement of the finger-withdrawal reflex?
steps: No. The stimulus is seen and the catch involves a deliberate motor response.
It uses nervous communication but differs from the specified spinal withdrawal pathway.
A measured reaction time cannot be relabelled as that reflex’s time.
example.explanation: Identify the pathway and choice involved before comparing speed.

practice.question: Must a reflex wait until someone decides they are in pain?
practice.answer: No. Its automatic spinal pathway can initiate withdrawal without waiting for conscious choice.
practice.explanation: Identify the pathway and choice involved before comparing speed.

commonMistakes: Do not equate all fast movements with reflexes or claim performed timing experiments.
